wordings: Diameter describes a length, while volume describes the segmented tumor in three dimensions. In a CT study of pancreatic cancer, these were measured separately.
A tumor’s diameter and volume describe different aspects of its size: a length versus its segmented three-dimensional extent. A pancreatic cancer CT study measured both separately.

In that study, a radiologist refined a semi-automated tumor outline slice by slice and measured maximum diameters in the axial, coronal and sagittal planes. Software then measured volume from the completed three-dimensional reconstruction.

The CT workflow used semi-automated segmentation, with a radiologist trimming the tumor boundary on each slice. Maximum diameters were measured in three planes—axial, coronal and sagittal—and volume was measured automatically after three-dimensional reconstruction.

The authors suggest that volume may better represent the full extent of an irregular lesion. That is their rationale for volumetric analysis, not a guarantee that volume is always the better measurement.
For an irregularly shaped lesion, the authors describe a possible advantage of volume: representing its full extent. They present this as a potential advantage, rather than a universal rule.

The study was retrospective, came from one institution and included Korean patients with pancreatic cancer undergoing upfront surgery. Its findings cannot be applied directly to patients receiving treatment before surgery.

This evidence comes from a retrospective, single-institution study of Korean pancreatic cancer patients undergoing upfront surgery; the authors caution against directly applying the findings to patients receiving treatment before surgery.
